newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Institution sells SPX calls.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Institution sells SPX calls.

text.p: A U.S. institutional investor was selling S&P 500 index SPX near-the-money calls, while other investors and traders were waiting for the last hour of trade before moving, dealers said Thursday.
The SPX July 910 calls traded more than 19,100 contracts by 1200 CDT/1700 GMT, far outdistancing volume in any other major index option.
The option, which was down a point at 11, had open interest of 24,570 contracts.
"There was a big seller of those," one index option trader said, adding that trading was otherwise quiet.
The spot SPX was up 3.13 at 910.67, moving toward the top end of its 904.31 to 913.18 intraday range.
September S&P 500 futures were unchanged at 918, also near the top of their intraday range of 911 to 921.
A trader in S&P 500 futures options at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange said that after a flurry of activity in early trading, turnover had trailed off by midday.
"We had aggressive call buying in the August 950s and 960s," he said, explaining that two firms were facilitating the trade, most likely for one large investor.
"Volatility's firm, nothing out of the ordinary," he added.
But dealers said the midday lull was probably just a pause before last-hour fireworks.
Over the last few weeks if not months, the market's volatility in the last hour of trading has increased dramatically, traders said.
"There are traders who are actually not coming in until later on," the index trader said. "It doesn't matter what you've seen up until the last hour."
He said the phenomenon was not brand new, but the amount of "radical" change in that period was different.
But he added that on a relative scale, the increased volatility was probably not as great as it seems.
"Relative to how high we are, the amount of real volatility and market change is probably lower" than in the past, he said.
The trader at the CME agreed that late-session volatility was picking up and said it usually happened once the bond market closed.
"You can almost bank on it," he said. "As soon as those bonds close, the S&Ps go crazy."
Jerry Hegarty, an options analyst at Thomson Financial Services, said late-session strength was a hallmark of a solid bull market.
In a report, he noted that on Wednesday, S&P 500 futures rallied in the last half-hour of trading to close 11.50 points off their session low.
"In the past that quick, sharp lift has served as a 'bear trap' where the market began a rally phase," he said.
